frameworks.name: Seven Sellable Categories
frameworks.definition: A taxonomy of value types that can be monetized: products (physical/digital), services (physical/digital), access (physical/digital), attention (physical/digital), risk (physical/digital), money (physical/digital), and endorsement/brand (physical/digital).

frameworks.name: Delivery Cube
frameworks.definition: A six-dimensional framework for scaling delivery: audience scale (one-to-one, small group, one-to-many), delivery model (DIY, DWI, done-for-you), support medium (chat, email, phone, Zoom), consumption format (visual, audio, live, recorded, text), speed and convenience (24/7 vs. scheduled, response time), and price-value testing (10x and 1/10th scenarios).

claims.text: There are exactly seven categories of things that can be sold: products, services, access, attention, risk, money, and endorsement/brand. Each category has both physical and digital formats, yielding fourteen distinct sellable types (Alex Hormozi, University of Texas entrepreneurship guest lecture).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: For a first-time entrepreneur with minimal capital (e.g., $100), selling time-based services is typically the only viable entry point, as most physical products and software-based digital products require upfront capital.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: no existing inventory or product base
claims.mechanism: Capital scarcity precludes physical product inventory and software development; services require only time and existing knowledge.
bounded_by: Does not apply to entrepreneurs with access to startup capital or existing product inventory
Does not apply to digital product resellers with pre-existing content

claims.text: Your competitive advantage as a first-time entrepreneur lies in knowledge acquired through osmosis—your parents' or mentors' professions, odd jobs, and exposure to their work—even if you haven't formalized that knowledge as experience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Informal exposure to domain knowledge creates unconscious competence that can be monetized by explicitly packaging and selling it; this tacit knowledge is a competitive moat against newcomers to that domain.
bounded_by: Requires ability to articulate or reframe informal knowledge into a coherent offering

claims.text: The "sweet spot" for an early-stage founder is identifying the person you provide the most value to for the least amount of money, then packaging and selling that specific solution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Targeting high-value-to-customer, low-cost-to-deliver segments maximizes profit margin per unit of work and creates a defensible market entry point.

claims.text: One-to-one, small-group, and one-to-many delivery formats carry different value propositions and scaling characteristics: one-to-one (highest per-unit value, lowest scale) through one-to-many (lowest per-unit value, highest scale).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Increasing audience size reduces perceived personalization and exclusivity, decreasing willingness-to-pay, but increases total addressable market.

numbers.axis: delivery format by audience scale and perceived value

claims.text: Do-it-yourself delivery models scale infinitely but carry lower perceived value; done-with-you models occupy the middle ground between scale and value; done-for-you models carry the highest perceived value but are the hardest to deliver and least scalable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customer perception of effort and personalization required from the seller correlates with perceived value; higher perceived seller investment justifies premium pricing despite reduced scalability.
bounded_by: Trade-offs between scalability and value perception; simultaneously optimizing both is not possible

claims.text: Support delivery medium determines scalability: email support is most scalable but least valuable; real-time Zoom availability is least scalable but most valuable. Intermediate options (chat, phone) position between these extremes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customer perception of seller availability and responsiveness drives value perception; synchronous real-time support signals higher commitment and exclusivity.

claims.text: Content consumption format affects perceived value and scalability: live in-person is most valuable and least scalable; recorded digital is most scalable but least valuable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Live and in-person contexts signal real-time personalization and exclusivity; recorded and digital formats enable unlimited reproduction but signal commodity status.

claims.text: Speed and convenience dimensions have two operational extremes: either overstaffing to eliminate customer wait (incurring organizational inefficiency for customer convenience), or full staff utilization with minimal wait times (passing inefficiency onto customers).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Efficiency and convenience are inverse levers; optimizing both simultaneously requires premium pricing to absorb the cost of maintained capacity.
bounded_by: Both extremes have produced wildly successful companies; choice is strategic, not absolute

claims.text: The 10x price test: if you were to charge 10 times your current price, what about your offering would need to change to justify that increase? This reframes pricing psychology from cost-plus to value-plus thinking.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: pricing strategy and business model design
claims.mechanism: Forcing a founder to articulate value-justification at a higher price point breaks cost-based thinking and reveals the actual value levers available in the current offering.

claims.text: The 1/10th price test: if you had to deliver the same or more value at one-tenth your current price, what low-cost or zero-cost value additions could you make? This reveals hidden value propositions and productization opportunities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: pricing strategy and scaling to mass market
claims.mechanism: Forcing a founder to deliver existing value at lower cost reveals which value elements are actual moats versus which are costly inefficiencies; identifies automation and elimination opportunities.

claims.text: Multiple categories can be combined in a single offer (e.g., a rock concert sells access to an experience, plus physical products like drinks and t-shirts, plus digital versions of the recording), multiplying perceived value and revenue streams.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Layering multiple value categories from the seven-category framework into a single customer interaction leverages the same audience and delivery vehicle multiple times.

claims.text: Selecting which category to sell from the seven options depends primarily on two factors: (1) resources you have access to, and (2) problems you can solve with those resources relative to the size of the problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Matching offering selection to resource availability and demonstrable skill creates natural defensibility and reduces competition; matching to problem size ensures addressable market.

examples.text: If your mother is an eye surgeon, you have accumulated knowledge about eyes and optometry through osmosis—exposure to her conversations, tools, and decision-making—that gives you competitive advantage in selling eye-care-related services compared to someone without that background, even if you haven't formally trained as an eye care professional.

If your father was a mechanic, you understand automotive repair concepts (e.g., carburetors) from exposure to his work, creating tacit knowledge that can be repackaged and sold as automotive service or education.

A rock concert exemplifies multi-category monetization: the primary offering is access to the live experience; concurrent offerings include physical products (drinks, t-shirts) and digital products (recorded versions of the concert). A single customer interaction generates revenue across three of the seven categories.

A call-review service (where a coach provides one-on-one feedback on recorded sales calls) delivers small-group value through highly personalized support, contrasting with a webinar to 1,000 people where feedback is generic. The former commands premium pricing; the latter captures volume.

practices.text: When choosing what to sell as a first-time entrepreneur, audit your family's professions and your own background for domains where you have informal knowledge through osmosis, and prioritize selling solutions in that domain first.
For early-stage founders, identify the person or segment where you deliver the most value for the least cost to deliver, and package that into your initial offering.
When designing a new offering, run both the 10x price test and the 1/10th price test to identify hidden value levers and productization opportunities.
Consider layering multiple sellable categories from the seven-category framework into a single customer experience to multiply revenue streams.

For service businesses, explicitly choose your position on the delivery cube dimensions (audience scale, DIY vs. DWI vs. done-for-you, support medium, consumption format, speed/convenience, price-value ratio) rather than defaulting to all-things-to-all-people.
